title: Why Don't 10,000 Starlings Ever Crash? 🐦
description:
Why don't starlings crash into each other in a murmuration? Each bird tracks only about seven nearest neighbours, so a turn ripples through the flock as a wave that travels roughly three times faster than one bird can react.

topic: Why don't birds fly into each other in a flock?
script: You'd crash in this flock, but ten thousand starlings never do. They swerve just inches apart, so why don't they slam into each other? There's no leader giving orders. Instead, each starling watches about seven neighbours. Close or far, it doesn't matter, it's always roughly seven. It copies their speed and their turns, and keeps a tiny gap. So when one bird turns, its seven neighbours turn too, then their neighbours, and the turn ripples through the flock like a wave. Scientists found that wave travels about three times faster than a single bird can react. Each bird sees it coming, like dancers in a chorus line. And seven seems to be the sweet spot, enough to stay together, without watching everyone at once. So could you dodge ten thousand people watching just seven?
key_facts: Each starling in a flock interacts with about 6-7 nearest neighbours regardless of distance (Ballerini et al., PNAS 2008; Young et al. 2013).
There is no leader; the flock's turns emerge from local copying of speed and direction.
Maneuver waves spread through flocks about three times faster than a single bird's reaction time, as birds anticipate the oncoming wave like a chorus line (Potts, Nature 1984).
Seven neighbours balances group cohesion against the effort of tracking others (Princeton, 2013).
